newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean worker sets self on fire in protest.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean worker sets self on fire in protest.

text.p: A South Korean worker set fire to himself during a clash between strikers from the Hyundai Group and riot police in the southeast city of Ulsan on Friday, a Hyundai union official said.

The worker was rushed to hospital and it was not clear whether he was dead or alive, said the official, who declined to be named. Hyundai workers have been at the forefront of strikes called in protest against a new labour law.
The union official identified the man as Jung Jae-sung, 33.

Later, a hospital official in Ulsan said the worker was alive but in critical condition with burns to about 30 percent of his body. Three other people were injured during the incident, the official said.
It is the first serious injury reported since strikes erupted on December 26.
Ulsan is the home of Hyundai, one of South Korea's biggest industrial groups.

He said rapid wage increases were a major factor hampering the country's economic competitiveness. The average wage for manufacturing workers was 1.7 times per capita income in South Korea against 1.2 times in the United States or Japan, he said.

"Many businessmen complain it is difficult to do business in South Korea, and set up plants in Wales, Scotland and other foreign countries," he added. "There is no customer in the world who wants to buy products out of plants where petrol bombs fly because of violent labour disputes."
But Jin rejected allegations by the Brussels-based ICFTU that the new legislation was a step backward for workers. "There is nothing in the new law that worsens the rights of workers," he said.

He noted that the new law allowed unions to be involved in political activity, removed provisions barring outside intervention in labour disputes and opened the way for multiple union representation from 2002.

"The ICFTU is only looking at one side of the issue, focusing on civil servants and teachers. People from the American Chamber of Commerce and investors in Korea complain about the rigid labour market," he said.
